# Urbanization in the United States

Urbanization in the United States

|     |     |
| --- | --- |
| ![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Ambox_current_red_Americas.svg/120px-Ambox_current_red_Americas.svg.png) | Parts of this article (those related to intro and Urbanization section) need to be **updated**. The reason given is: **Referenced primarily to the 2010 census, when the 2020 now exists.**. Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information._(December 2024)_ |

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Urban_and_rural_populations_in_the_United_States_%28US_Census_Bureau_%281790_to_2010%29%29%2C_OWID.svg/960px-Urban_and_rural_populations_in_the_United_States_%28US_Census_Bureau_%281790_to_2010%29%29%2C_OWID.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Urban_and_rural_populations_in_the_United_States_(US_Census_Bureau_(1790_to_2010)),_OWID.svg) Urban and rural populations in the United States (1790 to 2010)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-1)[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Template_map_of_U.S._states_and_District_of_Columbia.svg/960px-Template_map_of_U.S._states_and_District_of_Columbia.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Template_map_of_U.S._states_and_District_of_Columbia.svg) [Choropleth map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choropleth_map "Choropleth map") of urban population as percentage of U.S. states and D.C. total population in 2020

The [urbanization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization "Urbanization") of the United States has progressed throughout [its entire history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_States "History of the United States"). Over the last two centuries, the [United States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_of_America "United States of America") has been transformed from a predominantly [rural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural "Rural"), [agricultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural "Agricultural") nation into an [urbanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area "Urban area"), [industrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_society "Industrial society") one.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-main-2) This was largely due to the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution") in the United States (and parts of [Western Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe "Western Europe")) in the late 18th and early 19th centuries and the rapid [industrialization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrialization "Industrialization") which the United States experienced as a result. In 1790, only about one out of every twenty Americans (on average) lived in [urban areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas "Urban areas") ( [cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities "Cities")), but this ratio had dramatically changed to one out of four by 1870, one out of two by 1920, two out of three in the 1960s, and four out of five in the 2000s.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-main-2) According to the 2020 Census, approximately 265 million of 331 million Americans live in cities.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-:0-3)

## Urbanization

The [urbanization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization "Urbanization") of the United States occurred over a period of many years, with the nation only attaining urban-majority status between 1910 and 1920.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-main-2) Currently, over four-fifths of the U.S. population resides in urban areas.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-main-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-:0-3) The [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau") changed its classification and definition of urban areas in 1950 and again in 1990, and caution is thus advised when comparing urban data from different time periods.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-main-2)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-4)

Urbanization was fastest in the [Northeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_United_States "Northeastern United States"), which acquired an urban majority by 1880.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-main-2) Some Northeastern U.S. states had already acquired an urban majority before then, including [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") and [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island") (majority-urban by 1850),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-MA-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-RI-6) and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)") (majority-urban since about 1870). The [Midwestern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States "Midwestern United States") and [Western United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States "Western United States") became urban majority in the 1910s, while the [Southern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States") only became urban-majority after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), in the 1950s.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-main-2)

The Western U.S. is the most urbanized part of the country today, followed closely by the Northeastern United States. The Southern U.S. experienced rapid industrialization after World War II, and is now over three-quarters urban, having almost the same urban percentage in 2010 as the Midwestern United States.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-main-2) Just four U.S. states (out of fifty) have a rural majority today, and even some of these states (such as [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi")) are continuing to urbanize. Some U.S. states currently have an urban percentage around or above 90%, an urbanization rate almost unheard of a century ago.

The states of [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine") and [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont") have bucked the trend towards greater urbanization which is exhibited throughout the rest of the United States. Maine's highest urban percentage ever was less than 52% (in 1950), and today less than 39% of the state's population resides in urban areas. Vermont is currently the least urban U.S. state. Its urban percentage (35.1%) is less than half of the United States average (81%).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-main-2) Maine and Vermont were less urban than the United States average in every U.S. census since the [first one in 1790](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Census,_1790 "U.S. Census, 1790").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization_in_the_United_States#cite_note-main-2)

metadata.ogDescription: The urbanization of the United States has progressed throughout its entire history. Over the last two centuries, the United States of America has been transformed from a predominantly rural, agricultural nation into an urbanized, industrial one. This was largely due to the Industrial Revolution in the United States in the late 18th and early 19th centuries and the rapid industrialization which the United States experienced as a result. In 1790, only about one out of every twenty Americans lived in urban areas (cities), but this ratio had dramatically changed to one out of four by 1870, one out of two by 1920, two out of three in the 1960s, and four out of five in the 2000s. According to the 2020 Census, approximately 265 million of 331 million Americans live in cities.
